If the Hegelian-Marxist dialectic were merely a method, we could compare it to a pair of tinted glasses through which someone looked at the world. Looking at a white wall through blue lenses, they would describe it as blue; looking through red lenses, they would describe it as red.

But Hegel and Marx, and all their competent successors, never believed that they were describing what reality personally “looked like” to them. They claimed to describe what is: reality as it actually is. Hegel and Marx did not need to put on “dialectical glasses” in order to see dialectical reality. They saw it, so to speak, with their own eyes.

Contemporary bourgeois philosophers and scientists are therefore mistaken when they imagine that they can escape the dialectic—which they find extremely unwelcome—simply by “taking off their Marxist glasses.” That is, they think they can reject some supposedly invented “dialectical method” devised by Hegel and Marx which “distorts reality.”

In fact, the dialectic will remain there in reality itself. If it disappears from a particular study of reality, this proves only that the study does not correspond to reality—or at least that it fails to reflect reality fully, since it has overlooked one of its real and fundamental aspects.
In short, it is not consciousness of being that is dialectical. Being itself is dialectical.

It is true that “idealist” philosophers of every kind claim that being does not determine consciousness but that consciousness, on the contrary, determines being. They could therefore argue that even if dialectical consciousness comes first, and even if dialectic is a method, it can still “correspond” to “reality” precisely because reality is itself “determined” by consciousness—and therefore, among other things, by the method used by the investigator.

Fortunately, neither Hegel nor, still less, Marx was an idealist. Both fought “idealism” in every possible way. And since, following them, we know—as we will see again later—that “idealism” is false and impossible, we cannot regard dialectic as a method.

Consciousness and knowledge of reality—in the final analysis, discourse about reality—necessarily presuppose that reality exists independently of that discourse. Only discourse that “corresponds” to reality can therefore be considered true.

If dialectic were a method—that is, a property of discourse—it would introduce into the discourse something that was not present in reality itself. The discourse would then be false, because it would distort the reality expressed by its meaning.

If, on the other hand, we regard dialectical discourse as true, we must say that it expresses reality itself. Reality must therefore be dialectical first, while discourse is dialectical only because it reflects reality accurately.

To return to our earlier example: we see a wall as blue not because we are looking through tinted glasses, but because the wall itself is blue. Our glasses—that is, our “method” of seeing walls—are colourless and transparent. They do not alter the light reflected by the wall; they let it pass through exactly as it is.

The Hegelian-Marxist dialectic, then, is not a method, and in particular it is not a philosophical or phenomenological method. We can even say that Hegel was the first philosopher consciously to reject dialectic as a philosophical method.
As we will see, the discursive or logical confrontation between human opinions—especially philosophical opinions—is one aspect, or one expression, of the philosophical process.

A “thesis” expressed by one opinion is confronted by an “antithesis” expressed by the opposing opinion. Out of their “dialectical” interaction—that is, their conversational interaction, from the Greek dialektikos, or their discursive or “logical” interaction—there emerges a dispute. From this dispute comes another, “synthetic” opinion which somehow brings the first two together in a modified form. This synthesis then becomes a new “thesis,” and the process continues.
Plato’s Socrates drew attention to this phenomenon and was the first consciously to use it as a philosophical method, calling it “dialectic,” from the Greek verb dialego, “to converse.”

From his point of view, philosophical truth arises from this “dialectical”—that is, conversational—confrontation between opinions. So for the philosopher it is both necessary and sufficient to take part in such disputes, to provoke them, or simply to observe them in order to reach the goal: knowledge.

This view survived in philosophy all the way to Hegel. Philosophers after Plato certainly understood the necessity and meaning of this “philosophical dialectic” less clearly than Plato himself did. But in practice they all used it, because they too tried to prove that their philosophical opinions were true by critically comparing them with the opinions of other philosophers.

“Polemic”—discussion, dialogue, or dispute with contemporaries and predecessors—is a necessary part of all philosophical activity. In this sense, we can say that “Platonic dialectic” remained, until Hegel, the basic means or method for constructing a philosophical “system,” or whatever claimed to be one.

This kind of “dialectic” really was a method, because it tacitly assumed that the “dialectical” process—the dispute—took place only in discourses about reality, not in reality itself. Only opinions about reality arose, disappeared, and changed through the “dialectical” process. Reality itself was supposed to remain eternally unchanged.

Hegel, of course, did not deny the existence of this “Platonic dialectic”—the discursive or conversational comparison of one opinion with another, including philosophical opinions. But he understood and interpreted it in a completely different way.

Opinions are actually expressed by living people. They therefore form part of the historical world created by humanity, and so they are themselves parts of reality. Since reality itself is dialectical, these opinions must also be dialectical.

From Hegel’s point of view, philosophy as a whole is nothing but a single dialectical process. He therefore agrees with Plato that philosophical truth can emerge only as the result of this “philosophical dialectic.”
But Hegel also saw that this dialectic takes place independently of him. It takes place, so to speak, in a world “outside” himself and his own philosophy.

His philosophy must therefore describe everything that happens in the world. And so it must also describe the “philosophical dialectic”—the purely conversational or discursive confrontation between philosophical opinions.

But this dialectic is not the method of Hegelian philosophy. It is its subject matter, its object. Hegelian philosophy describes the dialectical development of philosophy in the same way that it describes, for example, the dialectical development of society or the State.

Hegel was also the first to understand that the philosophical dialectic—which, taken by itself, appears to be an endless process of pure conversation or pure discourse, something “ideological” or “ideal”—is only, to use Marx’s expression, an “ideological superstructure” built on the real dialectic of physical or material work and struggle. It is the reflection of that real dialectic in human discourse, or in the knowledge and consciousness that make discourse possible.

If we want, we can also describe this real dialectic as a “dispute” in which a “thesis” collides with an “antithesis” and, through their interaction, produces a “synthesis,” which then becomes a new “thesis.”

But if we use that language, we must remember that this real “dispute” is not settled by words alone. It is also settled by working muscles, acting in accordance with those words, and by the tools and weapons those muscles have made.
Philosophical truth therefore does not really arise from disputes among the “intelligentsia.” It emerges as the result of the physical efforts of humanity as a whole.

True philosophy proves its truth not by “arguing” against other philosophies, but by describing the entire process, which exists independently of it. This includes describing the process’s “ideal” aspect and, among other things, the dialectical development of philosophy itself.

The description must then show that this process necessarily leads to the emergence of precisely the philosophy that describes it in precisely this way. That philosophy must therefore be regarded as true—either definitively or, at least, at that particular stage of the dialectical process.

The dialectical process therefore takes place outside the consciousness of the philosopher who describes it. If the philosopher’s consciousness and knowledge of the process are themselves dialectical, and if the philosophical discourse built from them is dialectical too, this is not because of anything intrinsic to the discourse itself. It is dialectical only because it reflects the dialectic of its object: the thing of which we become conscious, which we know, and which the meaning of the discourse describes.

We can therefore say that before Hegel philosophers knew only the philosophical component of the “ideal” or “ideological” side of the dialectic. In other words, they understood dialectic only insofar as philosophers used it as a philosophical method.

Hegel, by contrast, was the first fully to understand what dialectic actually is. He stopped using it as a means of finding philosophical truth and began to treat it solely as an object of philosophical investigation.
We must therefore say that the Hegelian-Marxist dialectic is not a method, and that the philosophical and phenomenological method of Hegel and Marx is not dialectical.
So what exactly is this “phenomenological” method that Hegel used in his Phenomenology and that I, in turn, use in the book now before the reader?

The best answer, obviously, is to read the book itself. We understand the nature of a tool best by watching it being used. But even at this stage we can, and should, say a few things about the phenomenological method.
The most accurate description is that it is a purely descriptive method. It does nothing more than describe its object: the “appearances,” or phenomena.
The phenomenologist limits their activity first to “observing” phenomena and then to “describing” them. Their only concern is that the description should not “distort” what it describes.

On the one hand, the phenomenologist describes everything they see. On the other, they change nothing in what they see. They impose nothing on it, import nothing from outside, and add nothing that comes “from themselves.”
In short, the phenomenologist’s role is always purely passive.

We might compare the phenomenologist to the “ideal” lens of a camera that produced no distortion at all, and Phenomenology itself to a stereoscopic colour photograph of reality of the kind that can now be produced.
Phenomenology can therefore be called a “descriptive” science in the same sense in which we speak, for example, of “descriptive zoology, botany, or anatomy.”
The same principle applies. Phenomenology “describes” a phenomenon just as a zoologist might describe a cat or a geographer might describe Africa.

The difference lies not in the method but in the nature of what is being described. As we already know, the scientist always deals with certain “abstractions,” whereas the phenomenologist describes the most concrete reality possible.

The scientist’s description is nevertheless just as complete, relative to its object, as the phenomenologist’s, and vice versa. It is simply that the object described by the scientist is, so to speak, less complete than the object described by the phenomenologist.
Or, if we prefer, we can say that there really is a difference in method.

Before beginning to describe an object, the scientist first subjects it to a process of “abstraction.” They “isolate” it from a whole range of its aspects, setting these aside and retaining only the ones that particularly interest them.
The scientist then gives a complete and exact description only of this specially prepared object—this “isolated” or “abstract” object.
The phenomenologist does no such preliminary work on the object. They proceed directly to its complete and exact description.
So, like the scientist, the phenomenologist changes nothing in the object being described and adds nothing to it. But as a philosopher, the phenomenologist also removes nothing from it.
In principle, their description of the object is complete in the strongest sense.

The scientist always “abstracts” from themselves and from the fact that the object is “given” to them in a particular way. The phenomenologist retains this aspect too. In describing the object, they also describe how the object is “given” to them, and they describe themselves as the person who is describing it.
Everything just said about the phenomenological method also applies to the philosophical method in general.
The difference between philosophy in the narrow sense—that is, Cosmology and Ontology—and Phenomenology therefore lies not in their methods but in their subject matter and objects.

The object of philosophy is the existing world, both human and natural, together with the being that underlies it. The object of Phenomenology, by contrast, consists of “phenomena”: the “appearances” of the world to human beings.

As we know, a complete description of these appearances includes not only a description of what appears—the “appearance” in the strict sense, the phenomenon—but also a description of how what appears appears, and to whom it appears.
The phenomenological method is therefore simply an attempt to give a precise and complete, almost “photographic,” description of an “appearance” precisely as an appearance.
But this is only an analogy, and we must not let it mislead us.

It would be a mistake to imagine that the phenomenologist describes every phenomenon without analysis or selection, like a camera photographing everything that happens to fall within its field of view.

In reality, the phenomenologist makes a very extensive selection among “appearances” and describes only those that have been chosen. In this respect, the comparison with descriptive zoology is much better than the comparison with photography.

Suppose a zoologist wants to describe a cat “exactly and completely.” The first thing they do is make a <selection> from all the cats available to them. They choose “normal,” healthy specimens—ones that are, so to speak, “representative” or “typical.”
As a rule, they will not be interested in cats with badly developed tails or withered limbs.
But this first selection is not enough.

Once the specimen has been chosen, the zoologist must also decide at what stage of its development to describe it. They will describe neither a kitten nor an old, decrepit cat close to death. They will choose a cat in the prime of life.
The phenomenologist proceeds in exactly the same way.
Suppose they need to describe a particular stage of dialectical development—a particular “thesis,” for example.
This thesis lasts for a certain period. It does not spring fully formed into existence. It develops gradually and then gradually breaks down.
Like the zoologist, the phenomenologist will clearly choose to describe the thesis at the moment when it has reached its fullest development but has not yet begun to disintegrate.
And the same “thesis” may exist in several specimens, so to speak. It may appear among different peoples or even in different individuals.

Once again, like the zoologist, the phenomenologist chooses the specimen that seems most “normal” and healthiest—the one in which the distinctive features of the “thesis” appear most completely and precisely.
But the work of the zoologist—and of the phenomenologist—does not end with this selection.
After choosing a “typical” cat, the zoologist will also “schematize” it or, if you prefer, simplify it.
They may, for example, retain the cat’s skeleton and outward shape for study while ignoring the colour of its eyes, and so on.
The phenomenologist does exactly the same thing. They too schematize their object before describing it.

After selecting the most “typical” realization of the “thesis” under investigation, they retain whatever genuinely defines it as this particular “thesis,” as opposed to the corresponding “antithesis” and “synthesis.”
Everything else is set aside, just as the phenomenologist sets aside whatever also appears in other “theses,” “antitheses,” and “syntheses.”
At first sight, this may seem to turn the phenomenologist’s object into an “abstraction,” making the description incomplete and therefore preventing it from being “exhaustive.”
But that is not what happens.

By schematizing the object—the phenomenon—the phenomenologist is simply purifying it, so to speak, of foreign impurities and bringing out its “pure form.” Nothing is lost and nothing is removed from the object itself.

In this respect, the phenomenologist’s work of schematization can be compared to the work of a chemist preparing a “chemically pure substance” from raw material containing that substance by applying a series of reagents.
But the preparatory work of the zoologist—and of the phenomenologist—still does not end with this preliminary “schematization.”
The “schematized” object must also be “idealized” and turned into a “type.”
Everyone knows that very few people have genuinely “normal” eyesight. Most people are short-sighted, long-sighted, astigmatic to one degree or another, and so on.
It is even possible in principle that the “normal” or “ideal” human eye described by anatomy has never actually existed in any individual person.
Likewise, it is possible—indeed probable—that no living cat perfectly matches the “typical,” “normal,” or “ideal” cat described by our zoologist.
Yet this is precisely the cat the zoologist describes. They “correct” the specimen, so to speak, by “idealizing” the selected and schematized individual and turning it into a “type.”
The phenomenologist does exactly the same thing with the selected and “schematized” specimen of the thesis under investigation.

If some essential feature of this “thesis” does not appear clearly enough in the chosen case, the phenomenologist will “accentuate” it. And if this distorts the specimen in one sense, it does so only in order to “correct” it.
The result is an “appearance” that has never existed in reality with precisely this degree of exactness.
Once again, it may initially seem that the phenomenologist is somehow altering the object they intend to describe.
When schematizing it, they seemed to remove something. Now, when “idealizing” it, they seem to add something of their own.
But this is, so to speak, an optical illusion.

What the phenomenologist actually does is make the object—even if the expression sounds strange—more fully “itself” than it was before: in a sense, more real and concrete than it happened to be in any particular case.

We can compare this “idealization” to the work of a gardener who creates “ideal” conditions for a plant. The gardener protects it from wind, frost, drought, and so on, and gives it the soil best suited to it.
There can be no doubt that a plant grown under such “artificial” conditions will display the characteristics of its species more clearly than almost any wild specimen of the same plant.
The phenomenologist’s preliminary work, then—phenomenological “selection,” followed by the “schematization” and “idealization” of phenomena—does not distort them at all.
The resulting phenomenological description can therefore be regarded as fully exact and complete, insofar as it removes nothing from its objects, changes nothing in them, and adds nothing to them.
In principle, a phenomenological description, once the phenomena have been properly selected, schematized, and idealized, should have precisely this “photographic” exactness and completeness.

So if the description becomes dialectical, this can only be because the phenomenon itself is dialectical. And conversely, if the phenomena really are dialectical, the phenomenological description of them will necessarily be dialectical too.
